Context/Background:
Tumor-infiltrating B cells play a significant role in tumor development, progression, and prognosis, yet a comprehensive classification system is lacking. To address this gap, we present a pan-cancer single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlas of tumor-infiltrating B and plasma cells across a large sample cohort. 

We isolated B cells and plasma cells from 15 studies spanning 7 cancer types as data sources. After applying batch correction and integrating the data, we removed low-quality cells and determined the optimal number of clusters. Using standard Seurat methods for integration, clustering, and differential expression analysis, we confirmed the absence of batch effects, with no study- or cancer type-specific clusters. 

We employed a graph-based clustering method to identify TIL-Bs with recurring phenotypes, uncovering a total of 10 clusters. Step one of cluster annotation used canonical markers like CD19 and MS4A1 (CD20), which are prevalent throughout B cell development but decline in plasma cells. Markers such as CD38, JCHAIN, and SDC1 (CD138) are prominent in plasma cells, but less so in earlier stages. This revealed four B cell clusters, two intermediate clusters and four plasma cell clusters.
Prompt: Based on upregulated pathways and differentially expressed markers in each cluster, assign functional phenotypes to each of the 4 Plasma cell clusters (clusters 7-10).  Provide a discussion of the reasoning behind cluster assignments, highlighting important genes and pathways where relevant.

Introduction/Context  
A pan-cancer single-cell RNA-seq atlas identified four plasma-cell clusters (7–10) after integrating B-cell and plasma-cell data from 15 studies spanning seven cancer types. Clusters were defined by Seurat graph‐based clustering and annotated via differential expression (Wilcoxon, avg_log2FC) followed by GSEA and ORA. Below, we assign each plasma-cell cluster a functional phenotype based on its top upregulated pathways and marker genes.

Cluster 7 – “High-Secretory/ER-Mature Plasma Cells”  
• Key markers: MZB1, DERL3, FKBP11, SSR4, SDF2L1, XBP1, HSP90B1  
• Top pathways (GSEA KEGG_2016): “Protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum” (NES 5.60; FDR 1.7 ×10⁻⁶), “Protein export” (NES 3.00; FDR 0.088)  
• ORA highlights: Unfolded Protein Response, Proteasome, Oxidative Phosphorylation, mTORC1 Signaling, Interferon-γ Response  
Reasoning: High expression of ER‐resident chaperones (DERL3, SSR4) and secretory machinery genes (MZB1, XBP1) with coordinated enrichment of UPR/proteasome and OXPHOS point to fully mature, high-throughput antibody–secreting plasma cells under heavy secretory load.

Cluster 8 – “Stress-Response/Chaperone-Rich Plasma Cells”  
• Key markers: HSPA6 (avg_log2FC 6.65), HSPA1A/B, DNAJB1, HSPB1, ATF3, XBP1, JUN  
• Top pathways (GSEA GO_BP_2023): “De Novo Post-Translational Protein Folding” (NES 2.06), “Chaperone Cofactor-Dependent Protein Refolding” (NES 2.06)  
• ORA highlights: Spliceosome, Antigen Processing & Presentation, mTORC1 Signaling, Estrogen Signaling  
Reasoning: Massive upregulation of inducible heat-shock proteins and co-chaperones (HSPA6, DNAJB1) with enrichment of protein-folding pathways indicates a stress-activated plasma-cell state, possibly responding to inflammatory cues or proteotoxic stress.

Cluster 9 – “Class-Switched IgA/IgG-Secreting Plasma Cells”  
• Key markers: IGHA2, IGHG1/2/3, IGKC, JCHAIN, TNFRSF17  
• Pathway enrichment: no significant GSEA/ORA at FDR < 0.2  
Reasoning: Dominant upregulation of switched immunoglobulin constant regions (IGHA2, IGHGs) plus JCHAIN suggests a terminally differentiated plasma-cell population specialized in secreted IgA/IgG production, with the absence of strong stress/UPR signatures reflecting a homeostatic effector state.

Cluster 10 – “Metallothionein-High/Metal-Homeostasis Plasma Cells”  
• Key markers: MT2A (avg_log2FC 4.57), MT1X/E/F, LGALS3  
• ORA highlights: “Mineral absorption” (metallothionein genes; Adj P ≈ 2.6 ×10⁻⁴), UV Response Down  
Reasoning: Selective upregulation of metallothionein family members (MT2A, MT1X/E/F) and associated metal‐ion binding pathways indicates a plasma-cell subset specialized for heavy metal detoxification or redox buffering, possibly linked to oxidative stress adaptation within the tumor microenvironment.

Discussion  
Across clusters 7 and 8, we see two distinct secretory phenotypes: cluster 7 represents classical high-throughput antibody-secreting plasma cells with robust ER/UPR engagement, whereas cluster 8 appears driven by acute proteotoxic stress and heat-shock response. Cluster 9 lacks pronounced stress signatures but is defined by class-switched immunoglobulin expression, marking it as a steady-state effector pool. Cluster 10 diverges toward metal-homeostasis biology via metallothioneins, suggesting adaptation to the tumor’s redox/metal microenvironment. These functional phenotypes underscore the diversity of tumor-infiltrating plasma cells, from high-capacity secretors through stress-responsive states to specialized metal-buffering subpopulations.
